title: Unravelling the New Energy Vehicle Innovation Chain in the Pearl River Delta: A Hybrid Computational Intelligence Framework for Multimodal Big-Data Analytics
content: The new energy vehicle (NEV) industry is a strategic pillar of China’s manufacturing transition, and the Pearl River Delta (PRD) hosts one of its most concentrated innovation clusters. Yet the spatial layout, network structure, and policy drivers of the PRD NEV innovation chain remain poorly understood because the relevant actors, data, and methods are highly heterogeneous. This study proposes a hybrid computational intelligence framework that integrates kernel density estimation, spatial autocorrelation, social network analysis, and temporal exponential random graph models (TERGMs) to analyse multimodal data on 4,036 innovation entities, 95 patent-based cooperation ties, and 187 policy documents. Empirically, the PRD exhibits a ‘dual-core, core-periphery’ agglomeration pattern centred on Guangzhou and Shenzhen. The cooperation network shows intensifying small-worldness, with density rising from 0.22 to 0.32 and clustering from 0.56 to 0.68 across three observation windows. Six latent communities (modularity Q = 0.41) are anchored by universities and flagship firms. TERGM estimates indicate that non-subsidy policies have a stable positive effect on network optimisation (β = 0.87, 95% CI [0.75, 0.99]), whereas the long-term effect of subsidies turns negative (β = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.05]). Enterprise scale, university R&D strength, and geographic proximity promote cooperation, while technological distance inhibits it. Five robustness checks confirm the stability of these results. The findings offer actionable implications for spatial planning, intermediary support, and policy-mix optimisation in the PRD and a reusable analytical template for innovation-chain studies elsewhere.
